plants.name: Cercis canadensis
plants.description: Before its heart-shaped leaves unfurl, the bare branches and even the trunk erupt in clusters of tiny magenta-pink, pea-like blossoms. The effect is a hazy pink cloud drifting through woodland edges and suburban streets, and it is a favorite of early-season bees.
plants.bloomingSeason: Early to mid spring, typically April, lasting 2-3 weeks (later at cooler, northern or higher-elevation sites)
plants.location: Eastern and central United States, from the Midwest to the Appalachians
plants.funFact: Redbud flowers grow directly from old wood, a trait called cauliflory, and they are edible. They have a mild, slightly tangy flavor and are sometimes tossed into salads.

plants.name: Wisteria sinensis
plants.description: This vigorous twining vine drapes pergolas, walls and tree branches with long, fragrant, hanging clusters of violet-blue flowers. In full bloom, the cascading racemes look like purple waterfalls, and the scent is sweet and grape-like.
plants.location: Native to China; widely grown and naturalized across the eastern United States and temperate gardens worldwide
plants.funFact: Chinese wisteria twines counterclockwise, while Japanese wisteria twines clockwise. That makes the direction of the vine a quick way to tell the two apart. Mature vines can be strong enough to crush wooden structures.

plants.name: Camassia quamash
plants.description: Spikes of star-shaped, deep blue-violet flowers rise above grassy meadows and damp woodland edges. Together they look like a pool of blue water rippling through the grass.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late April through May, and sometimes into June in cool weather
plants.location: Native to western North America (Pacific Northwest meadows); popular in cottage gardens and meadow plantings in Britain and Europe
plants.funFact: The bulbs were a staple food for many Indigenous peoples of western North America. They were slow-roasted in earth ovens until sweet and soft, and they remain culturally important today.
